title: Where does oil come from? And why does the Middle East have so much oil?
keywords_tags: how crude oil formed in the earth
why middle east has so much oil
why only some places have oil
description:
Most people are taught that oil comes from dinosaurs — but that idea is misleading.

The vast majority of petroleum does not come from large animals. It comes from trillions of microscopic marine organisms that lived in ancient oceans hundreds of millions of years ago.

But ancient oceans existed across much of the planet… so why are giant oil reserves concentrated in only a few locations like the Middle East and Venezuela?

This documentary explains:

• how crude oil actually forms underground
• why only certain geological basins became oil superpowers
• why the Middle East holds such a large share of global reserves
• the difference between light sweet crude and heavy sour crude
• why some scientists proposed the abiogenic theory
• what chemical and geological evidence reveals about oil’s true origin

Using petroleum geology, geochemistry, and Earth history, we reconstruct the hidden processes that concentrated vast hydrocarbon reserves beneath regions such as Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Iran, Kuwait, UAE, and Venezuela.

Understanding where oil comes from also explains why global energy is unevenly distributed — and why certain locations became strategically important in geopolitics.

Atlas Veil explores the hidden systems shaping civilization.

description:

description:

————————————————————

How Did Humans Accidentally Invent Guns?
0:00 – The Shocking Truth About Guns
0:36 – The Accident That Changed History
4:33 – The First Gun Ever Created
6:04 – The Oldest Gun Ever Found
7:22 – The Cannon That Changed the World
10:47 – The Invention That Made Modern Guns Possible
12:27 – From Fire Medicine to Modern Firearms

All research and sources are linked below.

📚 RESEARCH & SOURCES:

▸ Chinese alchemists & the search for immortality — gunpowder discovered by accident while grinding sulfur, charcoal, and saltpeter chasing an elixir of eternal life. Several emperors died drinking mercury- and arsenic-laced potions. The mid-800s Zhenyuan miaodao yaolüe is the first written record, a warning not a recipe.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gunpowder

▸ Saltpeter (potassium nitrate) — scraped from cave walls, damp cellars, and manure piles. Holds oxygen locked inside the crystal, which is why the mixture burns almost instantly.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Potassium_nitrate

▸ The fire lance — first recorded in battle at the siege of De'an in 1132, where Song defender Chen Gui used bamboo tubes of fire medicine on spears against the Jin. Earliest depiction is a c. 950 CE silk banner from Dunhuang. By 1259 a barrel-plugging pellet was recorded, the first true bullet.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fire_lance

▸ Bamboo to bronze — tubes bursting under pressure drove Chinese metalworkers to cast barrels in bronze. The moment the tube became metal, it became a gun.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hand_cannon

▸ The Heilongjiang hand cannon — dated no later than 1288, the world's oldest surviving firearm. A bronze tube 34 cm long weighing 3.55 kg, no trigger or sights.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heilongjiang_hand_cannon

▸ Mongol transmission — gunpowder carried west across the Mongol Empire in the 1200s. By 1326 an English manuscript shows the first European picture of a gun.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gunpowder

▸ Orban's cannon & the fall of Constantinople — 1453: a Hungarian engineer built the Ottomans a giant bronze bombard, hauled by 60 oxen, that broke walls standing a thousand years in under two months.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople

▸ The matchlock — 1400s: the first true trigger, a metal arm that pressed the burning cord into the powder so both eyes stayed on the target.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matchlock

▸ The wheellock — c. 1500: a wound steel wheel striking pyrite like a cigarette lighter. Brilliant but too costly for armies.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheellock

▸ The flintlock — c. 1610, French gunmaker Marin le Bourgeoys for Louis XIII: flint scraping steel, cheap and reliable, the world standard for 200 years.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flintlock

▸ Alexander Forsyth & percussion ignition — 1807: a Scottish minister and frustrated duck hunter patented a chemical that ignited instantly with no spark, finally beating rain and the flash-delay.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_John_Forsyth

▸ The cartridge — by the 1860s, striking chemical, powder, and bullet sealed in one brass case, turning a 20-second reload into a one-second motion and opening the way to repeating fire.
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cartridge_(firearms)

————————————————————

PEOPLE & MOMENTS MENTIONED IN THIS VIDEO:

▸ The Chinese alchemists — court chemists paid by the emperor to find eternal life. Their exploding workshops produced the black powder that reshaped human history.

▸ Chen Gui — the Song defender of De'an who, in 1132, used the first fire lances recorded in battle.

▸ The Heilongjiang hand cannon — the oldest confirmed firearm ever found, a bronze tube from 1288 that fired a single projectile down a barrel.

▸ Orban — the Hungarian engineer whose giant bronze cannon brought down the thousand-year-old walls of Constantinople in 1453.

▸ Marin le Bourgeoys — the French gunmaker who built the flintlock around 1610, the weapon that armed Napoleon and the American Revolution.

▸ Alexander Forsyth — the Scottish minister whose duck-hunting frustration led him to invent instant, waterproof ignition in 1807.

————————————————————
